title: Who's Buying Lunch Solution
summary: Solution walkthrough: pick a random element from an array of any length by using names.length to scale Math.random(), flooring it to get a valid index, and returning a sentence.

concepts.heading: Picking a random array item
points: Array positions run from 0 to length - 1; names[0] is the first and names[4] the last in a 5-item array.
The function cannot assume a fixed size, so read the size with names.length and store it, e.g. numberOfPeople.
Math.random() * numberOfPeople yields 0 up to just under the length (for 5 people, 0 to 4.999...).
Math.floor() of that gives an integer from 0 to length - 1, exactly the valid indices.
Use that index in square brackets to fetch the name.

concepts.heading: Returning the result
points: Return (not console.log) the name concatenated with the rest of the sentence: " is going to buy lunch today!".
The leading space in the string literal separates the name from the text.
Test by calling the function repeatedly, with the same or different arrays.

code_examples.caption: Step-by-step solution

task.name: Who's buying lunch
task.starting_point: A whosPaying(names) function stub and an array of names.
task.goal: Return "<random name> is going to buy lunch today!".
steps: Read the array size with names.length.
Compute Math.floor(Math.random() * length) for a random index.
Return the name plus " is going to buy lunch today!" with the leading space.
task.expected_result: Each call returns a sentence naming a randomly chosen person from the list.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 15 - Intermediate Javascript/15.09 - Who's Buying Lunch - Code Challenge/script.js

pitfalls: Using length as the maximum index (off by one).
Forgetting the space before the sentence text.

playground.coverage: Matches the challenge closely, including the names.length point and the reusable random-item pattern.
gaps_and_ideas: Add a task testing the function with a 2-person and a 10-person list.
Demo idea: 'Pick' button repeated 100 times with a tally to show roughly even odds.
